clue.text: Drool over Irish whiskey?

indicators.note: drool spread over something covers it on both sides, so the second word sits inside the first

blocks.note: to drool is to dribble saliva
IR is the standard abbreviation for Irish

explanation.surface: Someone salivates at the sight of a glass of Irish whiskey.
explanation.walkthrough: The question mark flags that whiskey is only one example of the defined thing.
explanation.definitionFit: Whiskey is one kind of spirit, a distilled alcoholic drink, hence the question mark marking an example.

clue.text: Piers in medieval story's told to start without a meal

indicators.note: something told is spoken, so we want a word that sounds the same but is spelt differently
without means lacking, so the following little word is taken out of the word for start

blocks.note: Piers Plowman is Langland's 14th-century poem; Piers is the ploughman of the title
to launch something is to start it
the article, removed

explanation.surface: A literary note about Piers Plowman, the medieval poem, with a meal tacked on oddly.
explanation.walkthrough: The poem spells it PLOWMAN; said aloud it matches the modern spelling PLOUGHMAN'S. A ploughman's lunch is a British pub meal of bread, cheese and pickle.
explanation.definitionFit: A ploughman's lunch is a classic British pub dish of bread, cheese, pickle and salad, so it is a meal.

clue.text: Acknowledgement of item reviewed in Radio Times at first

indicators.note: at first points to the opening letter of each of the two words before it
reviewed is read as re-viewed, looked at backwards, so the word for item turns round
in places the turned word inside the pair of initials

blocks.note: first letters of Radio and Times
an item is a piece, as in a piece of furniture

explanation.surface: A programme listed in the Radio Times gets a critical review.
explanation.walkthrough: Radio Times is the BBC's TV and radio listings magazine; 'reviewed' looks like criticism but signals a reversal.
explanation.definitionFit: A receipt is a written note acknowledging that money or goods have been received.

clue.text: Conducts gender-fluid performances

blocks.note: trans is short for transgender, describing gender identity that differs from birth sex
acts are stage performances

explanation.surface: Someone leads shows exploring gender identity.
explanation.definitionFit: To transact business is to carry it out, the same as conducting it.

clue.text: Enraged criminal intercepted by motorway officer

indicators.note: criminal suggests something crooked, so the letters of enraged are bent out of order
intercepted by means something gets in the way, so a letter is placed inside the rearranged word

blocks.note: taken as written, to be rearranged
M is the label of British motorways, as in the M1

explanation.surface: An angry crook is stopped by a traffic officer on the motorway.
explanation.definitionFit: A gendarme is a police officer in France, a member of the gendarmerie.

clue.text: Blokes, gushing types so they say

indicators.note: so they say points to what people say out loud, so we want a word with the same sound

blocks.note: geysers are hot springs that gush water into the air

explanation.surface: Men who talk effusively, at least according to gossip.
explanation.walkthrough: Geezer is British slang for a man; 'gushing' suggests effusive men, but it means spouting water.
explanation.definitionFit: Geezer is informal British slang for a man or fellow, the same as bloke.

clue.text: King's boring flair for language

indicators.note: boring means drilling into something, so one letter goes inside another word

blocks.note: R for Rex, Latin for king
a nose for something is a flair for it

explanation.surface: A monarch is tediously talented at languages.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Boring' reads as dull, but it means drilling into.
explanation.definitionFit: Norse is the old Scandinavian language of the Vikings.

clue.text: Rodents a soldier's catching abroad

indicators.note: catching means holding something, so the soldier's letters wrap round the word for abroad

blocks.note: taken as written
a GI is an American soldier; the 's adds S
abroad can mean out and about, out in the open

explanation.surface: Rodents that a soldier catches while serving overseas.
explanation.definitionFit: Agoutis are burrowing rodents of Central and South America, related to guinea pigs.

clue.text: Exotic Parsee lady smiles briefly and I'm speechless!

indicators.note: briefly means cut short, so the last letter of smiles is dropped
exotic means strange and foreign, so these letters appear in an unfamiliar order

blocks.note: taken as written
the word loses its final S

explanation.surface: A smile from an exotic Parsee woman leaves the speaker lost for words.
explanation.walkthrough: Parsees are Zoroastrians of Indian descent.
explanation.definitionFit: The phrase is an idiom meaning I won't say anything, a promise of silence close to being speechless.

clue.text: Privy council against church welcoming ladies, possibly

indicators.note: welcoming means taking someone in, so the church letters enclose the word for ladies

blocks.note: con as in pros and cons, the case against
CE is the Church of England
the ladies is a women's toilet, which is a lav

explanation.surface: A secretive council opposes a church letting women in.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Privy' and 'ladies' both suggest toilets; only 'ladies' is used that way here, while 'Privy council' means a private meeting.
explanation.definitionFit: A conclave is a private, secret meeting, most famously the cardinals' assembly to elect a pope.

clue.text: England captain formerly on reduced grub

indicators.note: reduced means made shorter, so the last letter of the cricket word is cut off

blocks.note: Joe Root captained England's Test cricket side from 2017 to 2022
in cricket the on side is also called the leg side

explanation.surface: A former England captain is surviving on meagre food.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Grub' looks like food, but it is a verb meaning to dig about.
explanation.definitionFit: To rootle is to rummage or dig about, just as a pig grubs in the earth.

clue.text: Sounds like bad-tempered greengrocer's cross

indicators.note: sounds like says we want a word heard the same as the next one, not spelt the same

blocks.note: an ugly mood is a bad-tempered one

explanation.surface: A shopkeeper selling fruit is in a foul temper.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Cross' reads as angry, but here it means a hybrid.
explanation.definitionFit: The ugli is a Jamaican citrus fruit, a hybrid of grapefruit and tangerine sold by greengrocers.

clue.text: Categorise Harry Potter's eye

indicators.note: to harry is to harass or disturb, so these letters are thrown into disorder

blocks.note: taken as written

explanation.surface: A description of the boy wizard's eye, perhaps the one behind his glasses.
explanation.walkthrough: Harry Potter is a single name in the surface, but 'Harry' is the verb meaning to harass.
explanation.definitionFit: To stereotype people is to pigeonhole them into a fixed, oversimplified type.

clue.text: It's sickening to quote one contrarily

definitions.note: a descriptive phrase standing for a noun: a thing that makes you sick

indicators.note: contrarily means the opposite way round, so the combined words are read backwards

blocks.note: to cite a source is to quote it
one as a pronoun for the speaker

explanation.surface: Someone complains that being quoted backwards makes them ill.
explanation.definitionFit: An emetic is a substance that induces vomiting, so it literally makes a person sick.

clue.text: Dealer's staff on special drinks

blocks.note: S is an abbreviation for special
ales are beers
to man something is to staff it

explanation.surface: A trader's employees are on a drinks promotion.
explanation.walkthrough: In an across clue 'on' places the staff word after the drinks.
explanation.definitionFit: A salesman is someone who sells goods, i.e. a dealer.

clue.text: Directing evening out

blocks.note: first meaning: aiming, as a gun or an accusation is pointed at someone
second meaning: making flat or equal

explanation.surface: Someone is in charge of a night on the town.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Evening out' reads as a night out but means making even.
explanation.definitionFit: Levelling a weapon or criticism at someone is aiming it, and levelling ground is making it even.

clue.text: Not brought up to tease unmarried nursemaid

indicators.note: un-married means take away the abbreviation for married from the next word
to tease fibres is to pull them apart, so these letters are pulled into a new order

blocks.note: taken as written; M, for married, is removed

explanation.surface: A child not raised properly mocks the single nanny.
explanation.definitionFit: Unraised means not lifted up, the same as not brought up.

clue.text: One scoring equaliser in state, restricting England

indicators.note: restricting means hemming in, so the verb for state surrounds the abbreviation

blocks.note: to aver is to state firmly
ENG is the abbreviation for England

explanation.surface: A player scores the equaliser against England in some state of play.
explanation.walkthrough: An equaliser is a goal that levels the scores, so getting one is getting even, which is the avenger's aim.
explanation.definitionFit: An avenger evens the score by taking revenge, figuratively scoring an equaliser.

clue.text: Sound unit last month initially avoided calumny

indicators.note: initially avoided means the opening letter is left out of the next word

blocks.note: December is the last month of the year
libel is written calumny

explanation.surface: Someone escaped a slander charge last month.
explanation.definitionFit: The decibel is the unit used to measure the loudness of sound.

clue.text: Blocks, last couple of five digits

indicators.note: last couple of picks out the final two letters of the following word

blocks.note: the final pair of letters
toes are digits of the foot

explanation.surface: A note on the final two of five fingers or numbers.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Digits' suggests numbers alongside 'five', but here they are toes.
explanation.definitionFit: A veto blocks a proposal, so vetoes are blocks on something; as a verb, vetoes means blocks.

clue.text: Maestro cheekily clasping foot

indicators.note: clasping means holding tight, so the words before it hold the answer within their letters

blocks.note: the run of letters across the end of the first word and start of the second

explanation.surface: A conductor playfully grabs someone's foot.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Foot' is a metrical term here, not a body part.
explanation.definitionFit: A trochee is a metrical foot of one stressed then one unstressed syllable.

clue.text: Censor depressed writer

blocks.note: feeling blue is feeling depressed
a pencil is a writing instrument

explanation.surface: A gloomy author faces the censor.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Writer' suggests an author, but here it is a writing implement.
explanation.definitionFit: To blue-pencil a text is to cut or censor it, from editors' traditional blue pencils.

clue.text: Plenty of time to muse

blocks.note: an era is a long period of time
taken as written

explanation.surface: Someone has lots of time to sit and think.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Muse' reads as a verb meaning to ponder, but it is the noun for one of the nine goddesses.
explanation.definitionFit: Erato is the Greek Muse of lyric and love poetry, one of the nine Muses.

clue.text: Oddie's first swan not ringed?

indicators.note: first picks only the initial letter of the surname before it

blocks.note: Bill Oddie is a British TV birdwatcher
a pen is a female swan

explanation.surface: Birdwatcher Bill Oddie notes that his first swan carries no identifying leg ring.
explanation.walkthrough: Birds are ringed for tracking, but 'not ringed' is the definition: not encircled or closed in.
explanation.definitionFit: Something not enclosed by a ring is open, unenclosed on every side.

clue.text: A setter's retired to tackle good puzzle

indicators.note: retired means gone back, so the opening words are read backwards
to tackle is to grab hold of, so the turned words wrap around a letter

blocks.note: taken as written
the setter speaks of what is theirs as mine
G is the abbreviation for good

explanation.surface: A retired crossword setter takes on a fine puzzle.
explanation.definitionFit: An enigma is a mystery or riddle, something puzzling.

clue.text: Clearly bowled, as is fitting

blocks.note: B for bowled, the cricket scorecard abbreviation
rightly means properly, as is fitting

explanation.surface: A batsman was clearly bowled out, and deservedly so.
explanation.definitionFit: Shining brightly means shining clearly and vividly.

clue.text: Artist may use this daily fuel

blocks.note: a daily or char is a British cleaning woman who comes in each day
coal is a fuel

explanation.surface: A painter might use the fuel delivered every day.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Daily' reads as every day, but it is the noun for a cleaner.
explanation.definitionFit: Charcoal sticks are a drawing medium used by artists for sketching.

clue.text: Voracious guzzler originally quite thin

indicators.note: originally means at the start, so only the opening letter of the word before is used

blocks.note: first letter only
reedy means slender like a reed

explanation.surface: A greedy eater who was once slim.
explanation.definitionFit: A voracious appetite is a greedy one, craving large amounts of food.
